rationale: A wins because it stays inside the facts and turns the same announcement into three usable reporter shapes without pretending the market has already spoken. Its strongest line, "betting its network earns more as a utility than a perk," is a real finance angle with the right proof burden. B has good raw material, but "Wall Street hasn't repriced it yet" asserts a market reaction the update does not give, and "After Tesla" leans on an unsupplied comparison as if it were already proven.
gaps_in_A: "Rivian keeps owners cheaper as it opens the gates" is a softer duplicate of the premium-pricing angle; useful, but thinner than the finance and infrastructure angles.
"the way it has for one walled competitor" smuggles in an outside comparison without proof from the update; it is framed carefully, but still needs sourcing before use.
A could have made the consumer-driver access angle more direct: non-Rivian owners gaining 3,500+ chargers is a cleaner protagonist than existing Rivian-owner loyalty.
gaps_in_B: "Wall Street hasn't repriced it yet" is invented. The update says Rivian is public, not that the stock has or has not reacted.

"After Tesla" and "Tesla opening its Supercharger network was a major structural story" may be true context, but it is not supplied in the update; B treats outside market history as established evidence.
"That potentially changes the comp set and the investment thesis" overreaches without charging revenue scale, analyst reaction, or any proof that investors see Rivian differently.
The revenue angle and investor angle blur into the same P&L/valuation story; four angles here are not four clean stories.
